name: Use a ferrocerium rod effectively
blurb: The modern fire-starter: 3,000-degree sparks from a scraped alloy rod. It works soaked, in wind and in cold, and there is a technique that separates confident use from scratching hopefully.
gear: A ferro rod, 8 mm or thicker for a decent spark shower
A sharp 90-degree striker or the spine of a knife
Cotton wool, birch bark or fine tinder
steps: Check your striker: a square spine with a sharp corner throws sparks; a rounded spine does nothing. Sharpen it with a file if needed.
Prepare tinder first, always — a ferro rod lights tinder, it does not light logs.
Use the pull-back technique: hold the striker still against the rod and pull the rod back beneath it, which keeps your tinder pile intact.
Aim the sparks into the tinder from close range, no more than a couple of centimetres away.
Practise with progressively harder tinder: cotton wool, then birch bark, then feather sticks, then damp material.
Learn to shave a small pile of ferro dust onto stubborn tinder and ignite that pile with a spark.
tips: Scraping forwards usually scatters your carefully built tinder nest across the ground.
A new rod has a protective coating to scrape off before it sparks properly.
proof: One-strike ignition of natural tinder you gathered, in wind, three times running.
